newsitem.title: FINLAND: World steel consumption to hit record in 97 - IISI.
newsitem.headline: World steel consumption to hit record in 97 - IISI.

text.p: World consumption of steel products will rise 3.4 percent to reach a record 680 million tonnes in 1997, the International Iron and Steel Institute said on Monday.
It said 1996 consumption was expected to total 657 million tonnes, five million tonnes over the 1995 level.

In a statement on remarks by Lenhard Holschuh, secretary general of the institute to its annual conference here, it said strong housing starts and automotive sales in the United States would keep demand there around 100 million tonnes this year.
In the European Union, it said average economic growth would be below two percent, adding: "restrictions imposed to meet the criteria for joining the single European currency are a major influence".

But it said "it is now widely believed that (steel) inventories are back to normal levels, and the absence of their negative effect in 1997, together with real growth in steel use, means that apparent consumption next year in the European Union will rise by 5.7 million tonnes, or five percent."

Steel consumption in central and eastern Europe has slowed: "after more than 20 percent added in 1995, increases of only 2.9 percent and 2.5 percent are expected in 1996 and 1997, taking the area's steel consumption to 18.3 million tonnes next year".
In Russia, growth is expected to remain negative this year and next. "Steel consumption is around 17 million tonnes annually; about 60 percent of Russian steel is exported.

"Very little is known about the development of the steel market in the other republics of the former Soviet Union, but their combined consumption, including that of Russia, is estimated to be about 35 million tonnes," IISI said.

In China, the steel market has been burdened by high inventories which will hold apparent 1996 consumption to 95 million tonnes, IISI said. "However, the inventory rundown is now over, and 1997 consumption will probably rise to 100 million tonnes".

In Japan, consumption will probably rise by about two percent in 1996 from 1995 but high inventories will dent apparent consumption: IISI said falling demand from construction in 1997 would cut apparent consumption by almost one percent, to 78.6 million tonnes.
Globablly in the medium term, IISI said apart from cyclical variations it did "not see much change in the volume of steel consumption in the mature industrial markets".
It forecast an overall 1.8 percent increase in consumption to 714 million tonnes in 2000 from 652.2 million tonnes in 1995.

Growth would continue in developing regions, particularly in South America and China, IISI said, but added there are signs of maturity and slowing growth in the big Asian economies of Korea and Taiwan.
